fairest mode for another reason; if in an

ine them before I rose to address the Senate.

ican debt abroad, ten millions per annum

ty of such deduction; the debt exists and

needed; but certainly none can object to
the reserve of ten millions. We thus get
as said, a nett balance from our annual
exports, including profits, of 110 millions.

and more powerful than reason. Drunkenness
is man's own work. It is peculiar
to his kind. It is not found anywhere
else throughout the whole universe. A
Drunken man is the hardest and most difficult
thing in the whole creation for philosophers
to classify. Who can say to
what genus he belongs? In the whole
course of my examination and ample ex-
perience, and feeling too, am sorry to
say I'd have been unable to decide to
what he belongs. It is man; he has
not the feeling, the intellect, the heart, or
the form of man. That face and form,
shaped in the image of his Creator, he no
longer looks upward to the skies, as he
was made by his Creator to do. He
can't walk. It fuddles his brain, blears
his eyes, deadens his ears, swells his bod-
y, and dwindles his legs. What ruin does
it not work upon his heart and moral con-
stitution. All the rest it does one might
overlook. If it only made him sick,
destroyed his beauty, and sent him to a
premature grave—if it only dilapidated his
health, and took his life, we might forgive
it. Man must die, and what only accele-
rates this few days or weeks might be
overlooked. But there is the diviner part,
which, on the authority of revelation, was
breathed into him by the Creator, he
alone, of all creatures, becomes unhearted,
destroys his reason, his heart, and moral
organization. Nothing else destroys pa-
rental feeling—that feeling which, when
all hope of life has forsaken him, still
clings to him. It is alcohol alone that
has the power to do this. You may give
arsenic to a man, you may poison him,
still at the point of death he thinks of
wife and child, of his country and friends.
Alcohol can achieve what nothing else
can do; it can overthrow, destroy, and
ruin the immortal soul. What else can
poison the heart, and lift the arm against
the innocent? You may make man a
robber, murderer, an enemy of his kind,
but let him go to his wife and child, he is
still man. Nothing but alcohol can
destroy the chivalry of manhood, can raise
the arm of man against feeble, helpless,
innocent woman—nothing but alcohol
can destroy parental feeling. You may
have man suffering from disease, from
poverty, from crime, and bring him to the
immediate presence of death, and bring
him the infant bound to him by the strong
and indissoluble ties of parent, and still
his feeling will be drawn to him. Alco-
hol obliterates every trace of the great ori-
ginal whence he was taken and formed.
Gentlemen, I might descant forever on the
evils of alcohol, might trace its every
operation, might show the evils which it
brings, without the slightest particle of
benefit to counterbalance this enormous
evil. When I think of intemperance, I
trust to reason for its overthrow. The
time is perhaps not yet come, and there
will perchance be great struggle be-
fore the grand contamination is achiev-
ed.

the judicial tribunals of his country for the commis-

MR. A. believed seven years, when the thunders of elo-
quence of Edmund Burke and Robert Brindley
Sheridan were poured upon his head; he almost
thought that he was guilty of the crimes with which
he had been charged, so powerful was the eloquence
with which he was assailed. The eloquence which
the gentleman from Kentucky had now exercised
personally against him, under the profession of
having no personal feeling, was equal to that of
Burke and Sheridan combined. But he Mr. A.
did assure the gentleman and the House, that, no
for single instant, had the idea been impressed
upon his mind that he was guilty of any part of the
charges brought against him. Not for a moment
had he been driven from that sense of conscious
innocence with which he met this charge, coming
as it did, from the most extraordinary combination
of parties that had ever been formed in this House,
a combination of a most formidable character.

place from the State of Georgia. The first attack
upon him here had been from a Georgia witness (Mr.
A. recaptured the circumstances attending the
presentation of the petition and letter from Clarks-
ville, Georgia, so postmarked and mailed. A gen-
tleman from Maryland and Mr. Johnson, in relation
to the opinions expressed by the members from Georgia that
that petition was a hoax, had added fact unknown
to him Mr. A. that the petition and letter were
written on Congressional paper. Did the gentleman
say that he was privy to the composition of
these papers?

was understood to say, that he had not examined
the paper but he had been told that it was the
kind—that it gilt-edged, and that the signatures
were all in one handwriting. The impression of all
was that it was a hoax. He had never seen the
paper till he had seen it at the Clerk's desk. The
Representatives from the State of Georgia disclaim-
ed any knowledge of it. And (Mr. J. was under-
stood to say) if the gentleman from Massachusetts,
had taken the same precaution in reference to that
petition, as he had done in reference to the petition
pending—written to see if the paper was
genuine—he would have found out whether the
signatures were true or not.

to send to Georgia to do so. If it was a hoax, the
injury was the greater to his rights and to the rights
of his constituents, and the breach of privilege to
him was greater than if the paper had been genu-
ine. It, therefore, the gentleman's information
correct, and if the petition was on Congress
paper, what was the inference? That it was a
fabrication on the part of some member of the House
to draw him (Mr. A.) into the difficulty into which
he had been brought. It might be so in the usu-
al simplicity of his heart, he had received the paper
as a genuine paper, and he believed it to be so.

the purpose of explanation, he disclaimed any
knowledge whether the document was on Congress
paper or not, and said that he would disdain on the
half of himself and his colleagues, to say a word in
denial of the charge or insinuation (whichever it
might be) of this kind; yet he felt bound to say,
that the gentleman from Massachusetts ought to
have known, that he did know, that he had good
reason to know, in all at events, to believe that the
petition came from no meeting of citizens of Haber-
sham county, and must, if it from them at all
have come from a single individual. The gentle-
man must either have disbelieved what he (Mr. H.)
had stated to him, or at least have doubted the fact.

stant interruptions to which he was liable and re-
curring to the manner in which he had been cut of
at the very moment he was entering upon his de-
fence, fell back upon the assertion he had made as
to the combination of parties by whom the present
process was being carried on. He stood here he
said, upon the accusation of the gentleman from
Virginia (Mr. Gilmer) on the one hand, and the
gentleman from Kentucky on the other, both of
them being apparently extremely anxious to have
the question taken; that if he should be acquitted
on the charge of the gentleman from Kentucky,
there yet remained the other, upon which he was to
defend himself upon other grounds, against the
gentleman from Virginia. Who on this floor could
fail to be surprised to see the gentleman from Ken-
tucky and the gentleman from Virginia united to-
gether in this purpose of casting censure upon him.
The gentleman from Kentucky, the head of the
home squadron, and the gentleman from Virginia,
the nominal head, from the dignity which he
once cherished as Lieutenant Governor of Virginia.

I cannot but suppose, from the feeling manifested by you I had surmounted, and the perils I had encountered, that a description of my aerial excursion and adventures would be required by you. Floating away from you, it was a few minutes of o'clock with feelings of such delight as few mortal felt. It was my pride, my old celebrity at stake; it was all I asked, the wish to make you see that I knew my business; and had no intent, in my late unfortunate attempt to deceive you. My ecstasy was without bounds; it had wiped away the stigma of being pointed at, as one whose wish was to deceive the public. I had fulfilled my promise, and as pure in mind as the ethereal air floated in, sacred in the air and bathed in the mist of the cloud. At o'clock, wishing to pass into the clouds, I threw out a bag of ballast, weighing 15 lbs. Immediately on doing which, and noticing that I was approaching the river, was compelled also to send off the parachute with my last companion, the quadruped. I saw it floating onward toward the earth, and have learned since that it reached in safety its mother earth at about 10 o'clock, still having great ascendive power. I found the wind hauling to the northward, at 1.30 wind. W. had then crossed a river, tributary to the Alabama, and found myself bound towards Florida; at this time endeavored to ascertain the direction from compass, was pursuing but found it no avail; my balloon had a very great rotary motion, and as I turned so did my compass, without its magnetic influence tending northward. I had always desired to soar to as great an elevation as it is possible to arrive at, and having upwards of 90 lbs. ascendive power, determined to gratify my wish. Away I sped—continually ascending—leaving the clouds as far beneath me as they were above me when I started. Now began to feel cold, large drops of perspiration oozing from my skin, and tingling sound in my ears, as if something cracking in my head, a vacant feeling and difficulty of respiration—now very cold. The water in my bottle freezing, I took hold of it, in order to try if a drink would calm my nauseating feeling; it stuck to my hand, and drew the skin off as if blistered by fire. So uneasy, the drops of perspiration turned to liquid matter resembling yellow oil—my tongue became swollen, my nails and teeth were loosened, and every joint in me and all my energy appeared relaxed. I looked up, and saw the gas rushing from the neck of my balloon, and endeavoring to open my valve to effect its escape, but I had not strength to accomplish it. No, no! as whirling down I came, with feeling as if the whole system was driving to my head, I entered dense cloud, the substance which rushed past me with whizzing a sound, like steam from the escape pipe of an engine. of the West undertake the establishment of such work
As none have yet attempted. It, have determined
notwithstanding the infancy of our Town, and some
little diffidence in our own Abilities to commence a
publication of the kind. We enter the field not as
competitor with the long established and ably con-
ducted Magazines of the East; We cannot hope to rival
them, but with desire to contribute mite to the
advancement of Literature in the flourishing Territory
in which we reside. The GARLAND OF THE
WEST will be devoted to this object and we hope to
be enabled to produce such work will be a welcome
visitation at the resides our hardy settlers and
credit to the Place of Publication.


To further this object, we ask the support of the
friends of Literature, throughout the Country.


PLAN OF THE WORK.—Each number will contain
one sheet of twenty four pages (of the same size as
Graham's Magazine,) printed with good Type and
fair paper and will be made of choice Original
of distinguished Men, Together with Statistical ac-
counts of the West, &c. &c.


The services of several writers have been secured,
and it is the intention that the GARLAND shall be as
nearly as possible, Original. The selections made will
be from the best American Magazines of the day.


TERMS.


Single subscriptions, ONE DOLLAR per annum;
payable in advance. The low price of the work, will
compel us to adhere strictly to this Rule, and in no
case, will it be departed from.


To be BROUGHT FORTH, &c.
June next and will be continued regularly every month
thereafter.


All communications, to be directed Post paid to


EDW. N. YOUNG, Publishers.
N. FRANK,


L. Z. HARVEY,


Southport, Feb. 1842
